blocks.html: You met sideways throws in Horizontal Launches and angled ones in Launches at an Angle. An exam problem strings the pieces together: first the time in the air, then the distance, then the speed or direction at landing. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

Split the motion. Sideways, no force: $x = (v_0\cos\theta)\,t$. Up and down, acceleration $g$: $y = (v_0\sin\theta)\,t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. The two share only the time $t$. For the landing speed, energy is quickest: $$v = \sqrt{v_0^2 + 2gh},$$ whatever the launch angle.

blocks.name: exam-cliff-throw
blocks.cap: The blue arrow (sideways speed) never changes; the red arrow (vertical speed) grows by $9.8\ \text{m/s}$ every second.

blocks.title: A stone from a cliff
blocks.q: A stone is thrown horizontally at $15\ \text{m/s}$ from a cliff $45\ \text{m}$ above the sea. Find (1) the time in the air, (2) how far out it lands and (3) its speed at the water.
steps: (1) Vertically it starts from rest: $45 = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2$, so $t = \sqrt{90/9.8} = 3.03\ \text{s}$.

blocks.html: Using the whole launch speed in the vertical equation for an angled throw. Only $v_0\sin\theta$ is vertical. Check: a throw straight sideways ($\theta = 0$) must take the same time to fall as a dropped stone.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters on kinematics, energy and momentum

blocks.html: A ball launched toward a wall, a net or a fence asks two things at once: when does it get there, and where is it then? The sideways motion answers the first, the vertical motion the second. Builds on Launches at an Angle. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

$$t = \frac{d}{v_0\cos\theta}, \qquad y = (v_0\sin\theta)t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2, \qquad v_y = v_0\sin\theta - gt.$$ The sign of $v_y$ says whether the ball is still rising ($+$) or already falling ($-$). The top of the flight is at $H_{\max} = \dfrac{(v_0\sin\theta)^2}{2g}$.

blocks.name: exam-wall-shot
blocks.cap: The wall's distance fixes the time; the height formula then says where the ball is at that moment.

blocks.title: Over the wall
blocks.q: A ball is kicked at $20\ \text{m/s}$, $40^\circ$ above level ground, toward a wall $18\ \text{m}$ away. Find (1) when it reaches the wall, (2) its height there and (3) whether it is rising or falling.

blocks.html: Assuming the ball must still be rising at the wall, or at its peak there. Work out $v_y$ and look at its sign; the peak is at $t = v_0\sin\theta/g$, which may come before or after the wall.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters on kinematics, energy and momentum

blocks.html: Two stages, two laws. During a quick collision the outside forces are small, so momentum is conserved. After it, on a smooth ramp, energy is conserved. The trap is to use energy across the collision itself. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

Sticking collision: $$m_1v = (m_1 + m_2)V.$$ Kinetic energy is lost: the fraction lost is $\dfrac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ when $m_2$ starts at rest. After the collision: $\tfrac{1}{2}V^2 = gh$, so $h = \dfrac{V^2}{2g}$.

blocks.name: exam-cart-collision
blocks.cap: Momentum carries the pair through the collision; energy carries it up the ramp.

blocks.title: Carts on a track
blocks.q: Cart A ($0.6\ \text{kg}$, $3.0\ \text{m/s}$) locks onto cart B ($0.4\ \text{kg}$, at rest). Find (1) their speed, (2) the kinetic energy lost and (3) how high they roll up a smooth ramp.

blocks.html: Using $\tfrac{1}{2}m_1v^2 = (m_1 + m_2)gh$ straight from the start. That ignores the energy lost when the carts stick, so the height comes out too large. Check: an answer above $v^2/2g$ is impossible.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters on kinematics, energy and momentum

blocks.html: A loop puts two ideas together: energy gives the speed at the top, and the circle's force equation from Vertical Circles gives how hard the track pushes. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

Energy from the release height to the top of the loop ($2r$ up): $$mgh = mg(2r) + \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2.$$ At the top both the push $N$ and gravity point down, to the center: $$N + mg = \frac{mv^2}{r}.$$ Just making it round means $N = 0$, which needs $h = \tfrac{5}{2}r$.

blocks.name: exam-loop-track
blocks.cap: The object is slowest at the top of the loop. There the track and gravity both pull it toward the center.

blocks.title: A block around a loop
blocks.q: A $0.2\ \text{kg}$ block is released from $1.4\ \text{m}$ on a smooth track with a loop of radius $0.4\ \text{m}$. Find (1) its speed at the top and (2) the track's push there.

blocks.html: Writing $N - mg = mv^2/r$ at the top, as if the track pushed up. At the top of a loop the track is above the object and pushes down. Check: with $N = 0$ the equation must reduce to $mg = mv^2/r$.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters on kinematics, energy and momentum

blocks.html: A ball on a string, swung in a level circle, is a neat test of forces at angles and centripetal force. The tension does two jobs at once. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

With the string at $\theta$ from the vertical and $r = L\sin\theta$: $$T\cos\theta = mg, \qquad T\sin\theta = \frac{mv^2}{r}.$$ Dividing: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{gr}$. The period is $2\pi\sqrt{L\cos\theta/g}$, with no mass in it.

blocks.name: exam-conical-pendulum
blocks.cap: The tension's vertical part holds the ball up; its sideways part points to the center of the circle.

blocks.title: A ball on a cord
blocks.q: A $0.3\ \text{kg}$ ball on a $1.0\ \text{m}$ cord circles with the cord at $35^\circ$ from the vertical. Find (1) the tension and (2) the speed.

blocks.html: Using the string length as the radius. The ball circles the vertical line under the pivot, so $r = L\sin\theta$. Check: at a tiny angle the radius should be nearly zero.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters on kinematics, energy and momentum

blocks.html: A block on a spring is the model oscillator. Exam questions chain the period from Period of a Mass on a Spring with the energy ideas of Energy in Simple Harmonic Motion, then ask about timing. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}, \qquad \omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}, \qquad v_{\max} = A\omega, \qquad a_{\max} = \frac{kA}{m}.$$ Released from $x = A$: $x = A\cos(\omega t)$. The rest point comes after $T/4$; halfway ($x = A/2$) after $T/6$, because the block starts slowly.

blocks.name: exam-spring-oscillator
blocks.cap: The trace below the block shows its position as time runs down the page. One full wave is one period.

blocks.title: Pull and let go
blocks.q: A $0.5\ \text{kg}$ block on a $50\ \text{N/m}$ spring is pulled $8\ \text{cm}$ and released. Find (1) the period and (2) the greatest speed.

blocks.html: Thinking a bigger pull gives a longer period. $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ has no amplitude in it: a bigger swing is covered faster. Check with the formula before trusting your instinct.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters on kinematics, energy and momentum

blocks.html: Energy bookkeeping in three stops: the top of the ramp, the bottom, and the spring at full squeeze. Friction is the one thing that takes energy out, as in Friction and Energy. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

On a ramp the normal force is $mg\cos\theta$, so friction does $|W_f| = \mu mg\cos\theta\cdot L$. Then $$\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgL\sin\theta - |W_f|$$ at the bottom, and on a smooth floor $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

blocks.name: exam-rough-ramp-spring
blocks.cap: Friction pulls up the slope while the crate slides down; the smooth floor and spring lose nothing.

blocks.title: A crate into a spring
blocks.q: A $2.0\ \text{kg}$ crate slides $3.0\ \text{m}$ down a $30^\circ$ ramp ($\mu = 0.2$), then into a $400\ \text{N/m}$ spring on a smooth floor. Find (1) the work done by friction, (2) the speed at the bottom and (3) the squeeze.

blocks.html: Using $\mu mg$ for friction on a slope. The ramp only presses back with $mg\cos\theta$. Check: on a vertical wall ($\theta = 90^\circ$) there would be no normal force at all.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters on kinematics, energy and momentum

blocks.html: A free piston keeps the gas pressure fixed, so heating it is a constant-pressure process from Work Done by a Gas. The first step is always a force balance on the piston. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

$$p = p_0 + \frac{Mg}{A}, \qquad \frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{T_2}{T_1}\ (\text{constant } p), \qquad W = p\,\Delta V.$$ For a monatomic ideal gas at constant pressure, $Q = \tfrac{5}{2}p\,\Delta V$ (that is $\Delta U = \tfrac{3}{2}p\,\Delta V$ plus the work).

blocks.name: exam-piston-gas
blocks.cap: The piston stays balanced the whole time, so the pressure never changes; the gas just takes up more room.

blocks.title: Warming the gas
blocks.q: A $40\ \text{kg}$ piston of area $0.02\ \text{m}^2$ sits $30\ \text{cm}$ above the base, with outside air at $1.0 \times 10^5\ \text{Pa}$. The gas warms from $300\ \text{K}$ to $400\ \text{K}$. Find (1) the pressure, (2) the new height, (3) the work.

blocks.html: Leaving out the air pressure on top: $p = Mg/A$ alone. The atmosphere pushes down on the piston too. Check: with a massless piston the gas would still be at air pressure, not zero.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters 13 to 15 on gases and thermodynamics

blocks.html: An engine cycle on a $p$–$V$ graph turns into geometry: the work is an area, and each leg's heat comes from the first law of The First Law of Thermodynamics. The efficiency of Heat Engines then uses only the heat taken in. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

Net work $W$ = the area inside the loop (positive when it runs clockwise). For a monatomic ideal gas $U = \tfrac{3}{2}pV$, so constant volume: $Q = \tfrac{3}{2}V\,\Delta p$; constant pressure: $Q = \tfrac{5}{2}p\,\Delta V$. $$e = \frac{W}{Q_{\text{in}}}.$$

blocks.name: exam-pv-cycle
blocks.cap: The point runs clockwise round the loop: the gas does more work expanding at high pressure than is done on it at low pressure.

blocks.title: A rectangular cycle
blocks.q: A monatomic gas goes A ($1 \times 10^5\ \text{Pa}$, $2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$) → B ($3 \times 10^5\ \text{Pa}$, same volume) → C (same pressure, $5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$) → D → A. Find (1) the net work, (2) the heat taken in and (3) the efficiency.

blocks.html: Dividing the work by all the heat that crosses the boundary, in and out. Efficiency compares the work with the heat you pay for, $Q_{\text{in}}$. Check: $e$ must come out below 1.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters 13 to 15 on gases and thermodynamics

blocks.html: Two speakers playing the same note in step make a pattern of loud and quiet spots, as in Superposition. What matters at a spot is how much farther one speaker is than the other. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

Path difference $\Delta = |L_2 - L_1|$ and $\lambda = v/f$. $$\text{loud: } \Delta = m\lambda, \qquad \text{quiet: } \Delta = (m + \tfrac{1}{2})\lambda.$$ The lowest frequency that makes a spot quiet has $\Delta = \lambda/2$, so $f = v/(2\Delta)$.

blocks.name: exam-two-speakers
blocks.cap: Blue and purple rings are the waves from each speaker. Where crest meets crest the sound is loud.

blocks.title: Loud or quiet?
blocks.q: Speakers $3\ \text{m}$ apart; a listener $4\ \text{m}$ straight out from one of them. Sound travels at $340\ \text{m/s}$. Find (1) the path difference and (2) the lowest frequency that is quiet there.
steps: (1) The far speaker is $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\ \text{m}$ away, so $\Delta = 1\ \text{m}$.

blocks.html: Comparing a single distance with the wavelength. A spot $5\ \text{m}$ from one speaker tells you nothing alone; only the difference between the two paths decides how the waves meet.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters 16 and 17 on waves and sound

blocks.html: A wall turns one Doppler problem into two: first the wall hears a moving source, then it sends that sound back as a still source. Builds on The Doppler Effect. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

$$f' = f\,\frac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}$$ (upper signs when moving toward each other). A source moving toward a wall at $u$: the wall gets $f\,\dfrac{v}{v - u}$. A listener moving toward the wall at $u$ hears the echo raised again by $\dfrac{v + u}{v}$. Beats: the difference of two frequencies.

blocks.name: exam-doppler-wall
blocks.cap: Ahead of the vehicle the rings bunch up; behind, they spread. Purple rings are the echo from the cliff.

blocks.title: The driver's echo
blocks.q: A $500\ \text{Hz}$ siren drives at $20\ \text{m/s}$ toward a cliff ($v = 340\ \text{m/s}$). Find (1) the frequency at the cliff and (2) the echo the driver hears.
steps: (2) $531.2 \cdot \dfrac{360}{340} = 562.5\ \text{Hz}$, so the driver hears $62.5\ \text{Hz}$ of beats against the siren.

blocks.html: Putting the source's speed in the numerator. A moving source changes the spacing of the waves, $v \mp v_s$ in the denominator; a moving listener changes how fast they meet the waves, $v \pm v_o$ on top. Check: approaching must raise the pitch.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters 16 and 17 on waves and sound

blocks.html: The classic string-and-pulley setup ties the wave speed of Wave Speed in a Medium to the loops of Standing Waves on Strings. The hanging mass sets the tension. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.
$$T = Mg, \qquad v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}, \qquad L = n\frac{\lambda}{2}, \qquad f = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{nv}{2L}.$$ At a fixed frequency, $n \propto 1/v \propto 1/\sqrt{M}$.

blocks.name: exam-string-pulley
blocks.cap: Each loop is half a wavelength; the dots are the nodes, which never move.

blocks.title: Three loops
blocks.q: A string with $\mu = 2.0\ \text{g/m}$ runs $1.2\ \text{m}$ to a pulley holding $1.0\ \text{kg}$ and shows 3 loops. Find (1) the wave speed and (2) the frequency.

blocks.html: Treating speed as proportional to tension. It goes as the square root: 4 times the hanging mass only doubles the speed. Check units: $\sqrt{\text{N}/(\text{kg/m})} = \text{m/s}$.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters 16 and 17 on waves and sound

blocks.html: Lens problems chain the thin lens equation with the size and kind of image, then move the object and ask what changes. A ray diagram from Lens Ray Diagrams is the quickest check. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

$$\frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i} = \frac{1}{f}, \qquad m = -\frac{d_i}{d_o}.$$ Object beyond $f$: real, inverted image on the far side ($d_i > 0$). Object inside $f$: virtual, upright, enlarged image on the same side ($d_i < 0$).

blocks.name: exam-convex-lens
blocks.cap: Three easy rays: parallel then through F; straight through the center; through F then parallel. Where they meet is the image.

blocks.title: A candle and a screen
blocks.q: A $2\ \text{cm}$ flame is $20\ \text{cm}$ from a lens with $f = 12\ \text{cm}$. Find (1) the image distance and (2) the image height.
steps: (2) $m = -30/20 = -1.5$: the image is $3\ \text{cm}$ tall and upside down.

blocks.html: Getting a negative $d_i$ and calling it a mistake. A negative image distance means a virtual image on the object's side, as in a magnifying glass. Check with a ray diagram.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters 25 to 27 on optics

blocks.html: A lamp under water lights up only a round patch of the surface. The edge of that patch is set by the critical angle of Total Internal Reflection; inside it, Snell's law bends each ray as it leaves. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

Angles are measured from the normal (here the vertical). $$n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2, \qquad \sin\theta_c = \frac{1}{n}, \qquad r = D\tan\theta_c.$$ With flat layers in between, $n\sin\theta$ is the same in every layer.

blocks.name: exam-pool-light
blocks.cap: Orange rays escape, bending away from the vertical. Gray rays meet the surface beyond the critical angle and reflect back down.

blocks.title: The bright circle
blocks.q: A lamp lies at the bottom of a pool $2.0\ \text{m}$ deep ($n = 1.33$). Find (1) the critical angle and (2) the radius of the bright circle.

blocks.html: Measuring angles from the surface. Snell's law uses angles from the normal. Check: a ray going straight up (0° from the normal) passes through without bending.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters 25 to 27 on optics

blocks.html: Young's two slits turn a wavelength far too small to see into fringes millimeters apart, as in Double-Slit Interference. Exam problems then change one thing (the light, the slits, the medium) and ask what moves. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

Bright fringes: $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$. For small angles, $$y_m = m\frac{\lambda L}{d}, \qquad \Delta y = \frac{\lambda L}{d}.$$ Dark fringes sit halfway between. In a medium of index $n$ the wavelength, and so the spacing, is divided by $n$.

blocks.name: exam-double-slit
blocks.cap: Each slit sends out its own circular waves. On the screen they add up to bright bands and cancel to dark ones.

blocks.title: Fringe spacing
blocks.q: Light of $600\ \text{nm}$ passes slits $0.30\ \text{mm}$ apart onto a screen $1.5\ \text{m}$ away. Find (1) the fringe spacing and (2) the distance to the second dark fringe.
steps: (2) The second dark fringe is at $1.5\,\Delta y = 4.50\ \text{mm}$.

blocks.html: Counting dark fringes like bright ones: the first dark fringe is at $\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta y$, not $\Delta y$. Check: there is a bright fringe at the center, so dark ones must be offset from it.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters 25 to 27 on optics

blocks.html: A capacitor in a circuit behaves in two simple ways at the two ends of time, which is all most exam questions need. The in-between is the RC circuit curve. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

Just after switching on, an uncharged capacitor has no voltage: treat it as a wire. Long after, a full capacitor passes no current: treat it as a break. Then $$Q = CV_C, \qquad U = \tfrac{1}{2}CV_C^2,$$ with $V_C$ the voltage of whatever sits beside it.

blocks.name: exam-capacitor-circuit
blocks.cap: At first the moving charges go into the capacitor; as it fills, they switch over to R₂.

blocks.title: Before and after
blocks.q: A $12\ \text{V}$ battery, a switch and $R_1 = 20\ \Omega$ are in series with $R_2 = 40\ \Omega$ and an uncharged $50\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor in parallel. Find (1) the current at the start, (2) the current long after, (3) the capacitor's charge.
steps: (2) No current into the full capacitor: $I = 12/60 = 0.2\ \text{A}$.

blocks.html: Thinking current flows steadily through a capacitor. Charge piles up on its plates, but none crosses the gap; once full, its branch carries nothing. Check: in steady state, the circuit without the capacitor branch must give the same currents.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters 18 to 23 on electricity and magnetism

blocks.html: A charge crossing a uniform field moves exactly like a ball thrown sideways under gravity: steady along the plates, accelerated across them. The same splitting as Horizontal Launches works. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.
$$E = \frac{V}{d}, \qquad a = \frac{qE}{m}, \qquad t = \frac{\ell}{v_0}, \qquad y = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2.$$ An electron is pulled toward the positive plate; gravity is far too weak to matter.

blocks.name: exam-deflecting-plates
blocks.cap: Between the plates the path is a parabola; after them it is a straight line.

blocks.title: An electron beam
blocks.q: An electron at $2.0 \times 10^7\ \text{m/s}$ enters plates $4.0\ \text{cm}$ long, $2.0\ \text{cm}$ apart, with $100\ \text{V}$ across them. Find (1) the field, (2) the time inside and (3) the deflection.

blocks.html: Using $V$ where $E$ belongs. The field is volts per meter: divide by the gap in meters. Check units: $qE$ must come out in newtons.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters 18 to 23 on electricity and magnetism

blocks.html: A mass spectrometer sorts atoms by mass in two steps: a voltage gives every ion the same energy, then a magnetic field bends each into a circle, as in Charged Particles in Circles. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

$$qV = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2, \qquad qvB = \frac{mv^2}{r} \ \Rightarrow\ r = \frac{mv}{qB} = \frac{1}{B}\sqrt{\frac{2mV}{q}}.$$ So $r \propto \sqrt{m}$ for ions sped up by the same voltage, and the time for a half circle is $\pi m/(qB)$.

blocks.name: exam-mass-spectrometer
blocks.cap: The plates speed the ion up; inside the field the force is always at right angles to the motion, so it bends the path into a circle without changing the speed.

blocks.title: Neon ions
blocks.q: Singly charged neon-20 ions ($20\ \text{u}$) are sped up through $1000\ \text{V}$ and enter a $0.20\ \text{T}$ field. Find (1) their speed and (2) the radius.

blocks.html: Saying a heavier ion's radius grows in proportion to its mass. The heavier ion also leaves the voltage slower, so $r$ grows only as $\sqrt{m}$. Check: substitute $v$ before comparing.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters 18 to 23 on electricity and magnetism

blocks.html: A rod sliding on rails is the simplest generator. It joins Motional emf, Ohm's law and the force on a current, with Lenz's law deciding every direction. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

$$\varepsilon = BLv, \qquad I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R}, \qquad F = ILB = \frac{B^2L^2v}{R}.$$ The magnetic force always opposes the motion, so something must keep pulling; its power $Fv$ equals the heating $I^2R$. With a steady pull $F$, the rod settles at $v_t = FR/(B^2L^2)$.

blocks.name: exam-sliding-rod
blocks.cap: As the rod moves right the loop's area grows. The red dots show the induced current, and the red arrow the force that opposes the motion.

blocks.title: Pulling the rod
blocks.q: A rod $0.40\ \text{m}$ long slides at $3.0\ \text{m/s}$ on rails joined by $2.0\ \Omega$, in a $0.50\ \text{T}$ field. Find (1) the emf, (2) the current and (3) the pulling force needed.

blocks.html: Getting the current's direction backward. The induced current must push back on the rod; if your current would speed the rod up, energy would come from nowhere. Check with $F = IL \times B$.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters 18 to 23 on electricity and magnetism

blocks.html: The photoelectric effect shows light arriving in packets. Each electron gets the energy of one photon, as in The Photoelectric Effect; what is left after the work function becomes its kinetic energy. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.
$$E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda}, \quad hc = 1240\ \text{eV·nm}; \qquad K_{\max} = E - \phi; \qquad eV_s = K_{\max}.$$ Brighter light means more photons, so more electrons, but not faster ones.

blocks.name: exam-photoelectric
blocks.cap: Each wavy packet is one photon. The slowing voltage turns the electrons back; only those with enough energy reach the collector.

blocks.title: Ultraviolet on potassium
blocks.q: Light of $300\ \text{nm}$ falls on potassium ($\phi = 2.3\ \text{eV}$). Find (1) the photon energy, (2) $K_{\max}$ and (3) the stopping voltage.

blocks.html: Expecting brighter light to give faster electrons. The energy each electron gets depends only on the photon, so on the wavelength. Check: below the threshold frequency, no brightness gets any electron out.

sources.name: OpenStax, College Physics 2e (Rice University), chapters 29 and 30 on the quantum and the atom

blocks.html: Hydrogen's light comes from jumps between fixed energy levels, as in The Bohr Model. Each jump gives out (or takes in) one photon, so each pair of levels gives one line in the spectrum. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

$$E_n = -\frac{13.6\ \text{eV}}{n^2}, \qquad E_{\text{photon}} = E_{\text{upper}} - E_{\text{lower}}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{1240\ \text{eV·nm}}{E_{\text{photon}}}.$$ Visible light runs from about 400 to 700 nm. Atoms excited to level $N$ can give $N(N - 1)/2$ different lines.

blocks.cap: The electron drops from level 3 to level 2 and gives out a red photon: the brightest visible line of hydrogen.

blocks.title: From 3 to 2
blocks.q: Find the energy and wavelength of the photon from hydrogen's $n = 3 \to 2$ jump.

blocks.html: Using one level's energy as the photon's energy. The photon carries the difference between two levels. Check: a jump between neighboring high levels must give a small energy, and a long wavelength.
